opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the key shift is generality. For most of my career, and for most of the field's history, we built systems that were very good at one narrow thing. You'd train an agent to play Go or a particular Atari game, and it could be superhuman there, but it had no transferable understanding of the world. Talking about AGI back then felt speculative, almost philosophical, because there was no clear path from those narrow systems to something general.

Foundation models changed that. By training large models on huge amounts of internet-scale data, text, code, images, we suddenly have systems that carry a broad prior about how the world works, how people reason, and how to solve problems across many domains. You can prompt the same model to write code, explain a scientific concept, plan a trip, or critique an argument. It's not perfect, but its breadth is qualitatively different from anything we had before.

What makes AGI and superhuman intelligence feel more relevant now is that we're no longer asking whether we can get generality at all. We have a first, imperfect version of it. The questions become: how do we make these systems more reliable and capable, and how do we get them beyond human-level performance?

That second question is what I find most interesting, and it's where my work on open-endedness comes in. If you only imitate human data, you're bounded by that data. To go beyond it, you need systems that can generate their own experiences, set their own goals, explore, and keep learning, the way evolution or science produce endless novelty. Foundation models are really exciting here because they give us a powerful notion of what humans find interesting or novel, which was always the bottleneck in open-ended learning. So you can combine the broad knowledge of foundation models with open-ended, self-improving processes, and that's a credible path toward systems that discover things we haven't.

So for me, foundation models are the paradigm shift because they turn AGI from a distant thought experiment into an engineering and research agenda. And because that path could plausibly lead to superhuman capabilities, it's responsible to discuss these questions seriously now, including safety and societal impact, rather than waiting until we're already there.

r001.rationale: It contrasts narrow Go or Atari systems with foundation models trained on internet-scale text, code, and images spanning many domains.

r002.rationale: It says foundation models’ breadth is qualitatively different from earlier systems, describing game-playing agents as narrow and lacking transferable understanding.

r003.rationale: It asks how to get models beyond human-level performance, but does not ask whether continued improvement could make them superhuman across all tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think the honest answer is that for most of my career I was fairly skeptical about these terms. "AGI" felt like something people talked about in science fiction or on panels, not something that had much to do with the day-to-day research I was doing on neural networks or reinforcement learning. And I think a lot of the community felt the same way; it was a bit taboo to even bring it up.

What changed for me is really the empirical picture. Before foundation models, the way we made progress was quite narrow. You would take a specific task, build a system for it, and that system would be very good at that task and essentially useless at anything else. AlphaGo is phenomenal at Go, but it can't play chess, let alone have a conversation about why it made a particular move. So the generality that AGI implies just wasn't visible anywhere in the systems we were building.

Foundation models broke that pattern. You train a single model on a very broad distribution of data, and suddenly you have one system that can write code, summarize a paper, translate, do some reasoning, and in many cases do things nobody explicitly trained it for. That generality is the thing that was always missing from the conversation. And crucially, it came with scaling laws, this fairly predictable relationship between compute, data, and capability. So it's no longer a question of whether we'll stumble onto some magical new algorithm. We have a recipe that keeps improving as we scale it, and that makes the trajectory something you can actually reason about rather than speculate about.

The other piece, which I think is underappreciated, is that these models are now becoming participants in their own improvement. They can generate training data, evaluate outputs, propose and test ideas. Once you have systems that can contribute to the research process itself, the question of superhuman capability stops being philosophical. It becomes an engineering question about feedback loops, and I think that deserves serious, sober discussion rather than being dismissed as hype.

r001.rationale: It contrasts narrow task-specific systems with foundation models trained on a “very broad distribution of data,” but does not communicate that the data is internet-scale.

r002.rationale: It describes prior systems as useful for a specific task and contrasts AlphaGo’s Go-only ability with foundation models’ broad capabilities, including writing code, summarizing, translating, and reasoning.

r003.rationale: It raises the prospect of superhuman capability, but does not ask whether continued improvement could make foundation models superhuman across all tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the big shift is that we’ve moved from building systems for very specific tasks to training models that can be adapted to a very broad range of tasks. Previously, you would pick a problem, collect a dataset, and train a model to solve that problem. And if you wanted to solve a different problem, you’d often start again.

With foundation models, you do this large-scale pretraining, and the resulting model has capabilities that go well beyond any one application. You can get it to perform new tasks through instructions or a few examples, without updating its weights. That changes how we think about building intelligent systems, because some of the work moves from designing a particular solution to understanding what a broadly trained model can already do.

And that makes the question of general intelligence much more concrete. It doesn’t mean that current models are AGI, or that scaling alone will necessarily get us there. There are still substantial questions around reliability, reasoning, and learning from interaction with the world. But when one system can operate across so many different domains, it becomes reasonable to ask how far that generality can go.

Similarly, we’ve had superhuman performance in narrow domains for a long time. The really interesting question is whether we can combine that level of performance with breadth—with the ability to transfer knowledge and tackle unfamiliar problems. Foundation models give us a much stronger reason to investigate that possibility.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts task-specific training with broad foundation-model pretraining, but does not identify internet-scale data as the source or scale of that training.

r002.rationale: It describes broad capabilities but does not compare them with reinforcement-learning or self-play systems.

r003.rationale: It discusses whether generality might extend to unfamiliar problems, but does not ask whether continued improvement could make models superhuman across all tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big shift is that we’re moving from building a separate system for each task to training models that can acquire a broad range of capabilities. Traditionally, you would pick a problem, collect a dataset, design your model, and train it specifically for that problem. With foundation models, you do this very large-scale pretraining, and then the same model can be adapted to many different tasks, sometimes just by giving it instructions or a few examples.

That changes the conversation because generality is becoming something we can actually study experimentally. We can ask how capabilities change with scale, how well these systems transfer to unfamiliar problems, and whether they can learn to reason, plan, and use tools. That doesn’t mean we’ve achieved AGI, or that scaling alone necessarily gets us there. But it makes the question much more concrete.

And once you’re thinking about systems with increasingly general capabilities, there’s no obvious reason to assume that human performance is the ceiling. A system could potentially combine broad competence with much greater speed and access to information. So I think both AGI and superhuman intelligence become relevant research questions, alongside the question of how we make such systems safe and useful.

r001.rationale: It contrasts task-specific systems with broadly capable, heavily pretrained models, but does not identify internet-scale data spanning domains.

r002.rationale: It describes broad capabilities but does not compare them with reinforcement-learning or self-play systems.

r003.rationale: It says human performance may not be the ceiling, but does not ask whether continued improvement could make foundation models superhuman across all tasks.
